warnings: Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: Clarify that the tabular argmax example is a deliberately simplified form of behavior cloning and that practical behavior cloning usually learns a parameterized model capable of generalizing across observations rather than memorizing exact states.

State explicitly that a policy can be undefined for an unseen observation in this toy implementation, whereas a trained machine-learning model will usually output some prediction even for an out-of-distribution input; the real issue is unreliability, not necessarily absence of output.

Add a deterministic tie-breaking rule to the code or explain that dictionary insertion order currently determines ties. A visible tie policy would make the mathematical example and implementation more complete.

The lesson is strong but long for a foundational introduction. Consider trimming repeated explanations of unseen observations, copying behavior, and the absence of route planning, especially across See It in Your Head, Core Concept, Python Lab, and What Should Happen?

The optional challenge to add a demonstration beginning at (0, 1) should include a sample valid route or a note that the student must avoid overwriting an existing observation-action pair unless the intended effect is demonstrated.
Add one short activity comparing training loss or action agreement with deployment safety. This would help students distinguish copying expert labels from guaranteeing successful task completion.

The transition to drones is useful, but one sentence should distinguish imitation of pilot commands from learning a stable low-level flight controller; otherwise beginners may overgeneralize the rover example to thrust control.

The diagram.png instruction asks students to trace a signal, but the lesson uses it primarily as a conceptual schematic. Add a one-sentence question tied to a specific block so the visual has an observable learning task rather than only a viewing instruction.
For accessibility, ensure the inline diagrams use sufficiently large labels and high contrast, and consider adding a text-only route table for students who cannot inspect the generated visuals.

linkedin.title: Imitation Learning: Teaching Robots from Demonstrations
linkedin.description: A practical robotics lesson on behavior cloning, observation-action data, distribution shift, and a Python RoboRover simulation that exposes the limits of memorization.
linkedin.commentary:
Robots do not always need to discover behavior through trial and error. In imitation learning, they can learn from demonstrations supplied by a human or another expert system.

This Professor OS lesson uses RoboRover to make the idea concrete:

• Convert demonstrations into observation-action pairs.
• Build a simple behavior-cloning policy with action counts.
• Compare imitation learning with Q-learning.
• See how distribution shift and compounding error emerge after a small mistake.
• Run a complete Python simulation with unseen states and safety-oriented fallback discussion.

The most important engineering lesson is that copying expert actions does not automatically copy the expert’s goals, reasoning, or safety judgment. Try the lab, remove part of a demonstration, and observe what the learned policy cannot infer.
